t: In the Egyptian account Ramesses II was misled by two nomads sent by the Hittites, and his army was attacked while strung out on the march.
Almost everything known about the battle comes from Egyptian inscriptions and reliefs, whose bombastic tone is recognised; the Hittite side survives only in scattered references.
Neither empire could defeat the other in Syria, and about 15 years later they made a peace treaty that survives in Hittite and Egyptian versions.
dyk: A large replica of the Egyptian-Hittite peace treaty of about 1258 BCE hangs at the headquarters of the United Nations, as the earliest international peace treaty known to historians.
ev: The Hyksos' 15th Dynasty is expelled and the rulers of the New Kingdom begin reclaiming Egypt's borders
Ramesses II leaves Pi-Ramesses with four divisions and marches along the coast through Gaza
Two Shasu nomads give Ramesses a false report that the Hittites are far off at Aleppo
Hittite chariots cross the Orontes, scatter the Re division and attack the Egyptian camp
An Egyptian counterattack, the arrival of the Ne'arin and the Ptah division drive the Hittites back to the river
Ramesses II and Hattusili III make a peace treaty in the 21st year of Ramesses' reign

f.date: Year 5, third month of Shemu, day 9 of Ramesses II, generally dated to May 1274 BCE by the low chronology; the high chronology puts it about 20 years earlier
f.place: On the Orontes River upstream of Lake Homs, near the stronghold of Kadesh, on what is now the Lebanon-Syria border
f.sides: The Egyptian Empire under Ramesses II, in four divisions (Amun, Re, Set and Ptah) with Sherden troops and the Ne'arin; the Hittite Empire under Muwatalli II with allies, among them Rimisharrinaa, king of Aleppo. Chariots on both sides together are put at 5,000 to 6,000
f.outcome: The Egyptians drove the Hittites back across the Orontes, but the Hittites kept Kadesh. Modern historians describe a stalemate, and each side claimed the victory.
